In [[differential geometry]], a '''Lie group action''' is a [[Group action (mathematics)|group action]] adapted to the smooth setting: <math>G</math> is a [[Lie group]], <math>M</math> is a [[smooth manifold]], and the action map is [[differentiable map|differentiable]].

__TOC__

== Definition ==
Let <math>\sigma: G \times M \to M, (g, x) \mapsto g \cdot x</math> be a (left) group action of a Lie group <math>G</math> on a smooth manifold <math>M</math>; it is called a '''Lie group action''' (or smooth action) if the map <math>\sigma</math> is differentiable. Equivalently, a Lie group action of <math>G</math> on <math>M</math> consists of a [[Lie group homomorphism]] <math>G \to \mathrm{Diff}(M)</math>. A smooth manifold endowed with a Lie group action is also called a '''''<math>G</math>''-manifold'''. 

=== Properties ===
The fact that the action map <math>\sigma</math> is smooth has a couple of immediate consequences:

* the [[Stabilizer subgroup|stabilizers]] <math>G_x \subseteq G</math> of the group action are closed, thus are [[Lie subgroup|Lie subgroups]] of ''<math>G</math>''
* the [[Orbit (group theory)|orbits]] <math>G \cdot x \subseteq M</math> of the group action are [[Immersed submanifold|immersed submanifolds]].

Forgetting the smooth structure, a Lie group action is a particular case of a [[continuous group action]].

== Examples ==
For every Lie group <math>G</math>, the following are Lie group actions:
*the trivial action of <math>G</math> on any manifold;
*the action of <math>G</math> on itself by left multiplication, right multiplication or [[Conjugation (group action)|conjugation]];
* the action of any Lie subgroup <math>H \subseteq G</math> on <math>G</math> by left multiplication, right multiplication or conjugation;

*the [[adjoint action]] of <math>G</math> on its Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>.

Other examples of Lie group actions include:
* the action of <math>\mathbb{R}</math> on <math>M</math> given by the flow of any [[complete vector field]];
* the actions of the [[general linear group]] <math>\operatorname{GL}(n,\mathbb{R})</math> and of its Lie subgroups <math>G\subseteq\operatorname{GL}(n,\mathbb{R})</math> on <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> by matrix multiplication;
*more generally, any [[Lie group representation]] on a [[vector space]];
*any [[Hamiltonian group action]] on a [[symplectic manifold]];
*the transitive action underlying any [[homogeneous space]];
*more generally, the group action underlying any [[principal bundle]].

== Infinitesimal Lie algebra action ==
Following the spirit of the [[Lie group–Lie algebra correspondence|Lie group-Lie algebra correspondence]], Lie group actions can also be studied from the infinitesimal point of view. Indeed, any Lie group action <math>\sigma: G \times M \to M</math> induces an '''infinitesimal Lie algebra action''' on <math>M</math>, i.e. a Lie algebra homomorphism <math>\mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{X}(M)</math>. Intuitively, this is obtained by differentiating at the identity the Lie group homomorphism <math>G \to \mathrm{Diff}(M)</math>, and interpreting the set of vector fields <math>\mathfrak{X}(M)</math> as the Lie algebra of the (infinite-dimensional) Lie group <math>\mathrm{Diff}(M)</math>.

More precisely, fixing any <math>x \in M</math>, the orbit map <math>\sigma_x : G \to M, g \mapsto g \cdot x</math> is differentiable and one can compute its differential at the identity <math>e \in G</math>. If <math>X \in \mathfrak{g}</math>, then its image under <math>\mathrm{d}_e\sigma_x\colon
\mathfrak{g}\to T_xM</math> is a [[tangent vector]] at <math>x</math>, and varying <math>x</math> one obtains a vector field on <math>M</math>. The minus of this vector field, denoted by <math>X^\#</math>, is also called the [[fundamental vector field]] associated with <math>X</math> (the minus sign ensures that <math>\mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{X}(M), X \mapsto X^\#</math> is a Lie [[algebra homomorphism]]).

Conversely, by [[Lie–Palais theorem]], any abstract infinitesimal action of a (finite-dimensional) Lie algebra on a compact manifold can be integrated to a Lie group action.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Palais|first=Richard S.|date=1957|title=A global formulation of the Lie theory of transformation groups|url=https://www.ams.org/memo/0022|journal=Memoirs of the American Mathematical Society|language=en|issue=22|pages=0|doi=10.1090/memo/0022|issn=0065-9266|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

=== Properties ===
An infinitesimal Lie algebra action <math>\mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{X}(M)</math> is injective [[if and only if]] the corresponding global Lie group action is free. This follows from the fact that the kernel of <math>\mathrm{d}_e\sigma_x\colon
\mathfrak{g}\to T_xM</math> is the Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{g}_x \subseteq \mathfrak{g}</math> of the stabilizer <math>G_x \subseteq G</math>. 

On the other hand, <math>\mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{X}(M)</math> in general not surjective. For instance, let <math>\pi: P \to M</math> be a principal <math>G</math>-bundle: the image of the infinitesimal action is actually equal to the [[Vertical and horizontal bundles|vertical subbundle]] <math>T^\pi P \subset TP</math>.

== Proper actions ==
An important (and common) class of Lie group actions is that of [[Proper action|proper]] ones. Indeed, such a topological condition implies that

* the stabilizers <math>G_x \subseteq G</math> are [[Compact space|compact]]
* the orbits <math>G \cdot x \subseteq M</math> are [[Embedded submanifold|embedded submanifolds]]
* the orbit space <math>M/G</math> is [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]]

In general, if a Lie group <math>G</math> is compact, any smooth <math>G</math>-action is automatically proper. An example of proper action by a not necessarily compact Lie group is given by the action a Lie subgroup <math>H \subseteq G</math> on <math>G</math>.

== Structure of the orbit space ==
Given a Lie group action of <math>G</math> on <math>M</math>, the [[orbit space]] <math>M/G</math> does not admit in general a manifold structure. However, if the action is [[Free action|free]] and proper, then <math>M/G</math> has a unique smooth structure such that the projection <math>M \to M/G</math> is a [[Submersion (mathematics)|submersion]] (in fact, <math>M \to M/G</math> is a principal ''<math>G</math>''-bundle).<ref>{{Cite book|last=Lee|first=John M.|title=Introduction to smooth manifolds|date=2012|publisher=Springer|isbn=978-1-4419-9982-5|edition=2nd|location=New York|oclc=808682771}}</ref>

The fact that <math>M/G</math> is Hausdorff depends only on the properness of the action (as discussed above); the rest of the claim requires freeness and is a consequence of the [[slice theorem (differential geometry)|slice theorem]]. If the "free action" condition (i.e. "having zero stabilizers") is relaxed to "having finite stabilizers", <math>M/G</math> becomes instead an [[orbifold]] (or [[quotient stack]]).

=== Equivariant cohomology ===
An application of this principle is the [[Borel construction]] from [[algebraic topology]]. Assuming that <math>G</math> is compact, let <math>EG</math> denote the [[universal bundle]], which we can assume to be a manifold since <math>G</math> is compact, and let <math>G</math> act on <math>EG \times M</math> diagonally. The action is free since it is so on the first factor and is proper since <math>G</math> is compact; thus, one can form the quotient manifold <math>M_G = (EG \times M)/G</math> and define the [[equivariant cohomology]] of ''M'' as
:<math>H^*_G(M) = H^*_{\text{dr}}(M_G)</math>,
where the right-hand side denotes the [[de Rham cohomology]] of the manifold <math>M_G</math>.
